analysis.one_liner: Extends how long books, music, and films stay under copyright before entering the public domain.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House subcommittee without a vote, but an identical copyright extension became law in October 1998, adding 20 years to existing copyrights.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added 20 years to almost every copyright: works by living or recently deceased authors would be protected for life plus 70 years instead of life plus 50, and older works already under copyright would get their terms stretched by 20 years. It would also extend special federal protection for old sound recordings from 2047 to 2067. In exchange for that long lock-up, it gave libraries a narrow right to copy and share works in their final 20 years of copyright, but only if the works were no longer being sold.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of copyrights that were about to expire — record companies, movie studios, book and sheet-music publishers, and the heirs of authors and composers — would keep exclusive control of their catalogs 20 years longer, collecting license fees that would otherwise have stopped. Because the extension applied to works already created, the windfall went entirely to owners of existing material, not to new creators.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Record labels, studios, publishers, and copyright estates

how_it_helps.text: Owners of copyrights already in their renewal term would get 20 more years of exclusive rights, stretching the total term to 95 years from original publication.

Copyright in works created on or after 1978 would last the author's life plus 70 years instead of 50, and corporate 'works made for hire' would be protected for 95 years from publication instead of 75.

Owners of sound recordings made before February 15, 1972 — a class with no federal copyright term today — would see their protection extended from 2047 to 2067, two decades of additional exclusive rights.

Libraries and archives would gain a limited right to reproduce, display, and share works during the last 20 years of their copyright term, so long as the work was not being commercially exploited and copies were not available at a reasonable price.

analysis.who_pays: Readers, teachers, researchers, librarians, documentary filmmakers, and anyone wanting to republish or reuse older works would pay license fees or wait 20 more years for material to become free. The public domain — the shared pool of books, songs, and films anyone may freely copy and build on — is the direct loser, and everyone who draws on it pays.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public domain, and everyone who uses old works

drawbacks.text: Every book, song, and film whose copyright was about to expire would stay locked up for 20 more years, shrinking the public domain that future writers, musicians, and filmmakers draw on for new work.
The library exemption is narrow: it covers only works in their final 20 years that no one is selling, and only the library itself may use the copies — no onward distribution to the public.

Because the extension applied retroactively to works already created, it gave creators no new incentive to make anything new; copyright's stated purpose of promoting creation would not be served, only extended revenue on the existing catalog.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The one public-facing concession — a library copying right for works no longer sold — was small and tightly conditioned next to a 20-year lock-up on the entire existing catalog. The bill's benefits were concentrated (decades more exclusive licensing revenue for owners of works already made), while its costs were spread across everyone who reads, teaches, researches, or creates from older material. It was a retroactive windfall, not an incentive to create.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House subcommittee from March 1997 until Congress ended in January 1999 without ever getting a vote — but an identical copyright extension was enacted separately in October 1998.

narrative.text: Representative Elton Gallegly introduced the bill on February 5, 1997, with nine original cosponsors from both parties, and it was sent to the House Judiciary Committee.
On March 5, 1997, the bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property, the smaller panel that handles copyright bills.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings recorded, no committee vote, no House floor vote, before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.
By the time it died, the bill had attracted 24 cosponsors, split evenly between 12 Republicans and 12 Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Copyright holders won anyway: an identical 20-year extension passed Congress and was signed into law in October 1998, so this House bill's quiet death cost the industry nothing — the same terms became law under a different bill number.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Copyright holders — the same extension became law in 1998

for.name: Rep. Elton Gallegly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Copyright Term Extension Act on February 5, 1997 and rounded up bipartisan cosponsors

for.name: 24 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Howard Coble, Howard Berman, Bill McCollum, Zoe Lofgren, and Bob Goodlatte

for.name: Motion picture and recording industries
for.role: Major copyright holders, led by the Walt Disney Company and the recording industry's trade group
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for 20-year copyright term extensions to protect aging catalogs (Disney's earliest cartoons and pre-1972 recordings were the marquee beneficiaries)

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its intellectual property subcommittee on March 5, 1997 and never reported it back for a House vote

against.name: Library associations and digital-rights groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed copyright term extension as a lock-up of the public domain with a token library exception

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 24 cosponsors split exactly evenly — 12 Republicans and 12 Democrats — and the original cosponsor list included members of both parties, making copyright extension one of the few issues with even two-party support.

industries.industry: Record labels and owners of pre-1972 sound recordings
industries.note: The bill extends protection for recordings fixed before 1972 to 2067 — a 20-year bonus for owners of old master recordings, whose works could not enter the public domain until then.

industries.industry: Motion picture and book publishers holding older catalogs
industries.note: Films, books, and songs from the 1920s through 1940s that were nearing the end of their terms would have stayed under exclusive license for 20 more years, keeping license revenue flowing and cheaper public reuse off the table.

industries.industry: Estates and heirs of authors and composers
industries.note: Copyright lasting life plus 70 years instead of life plus 50 adds two decades of royalty income for the families of writers and songwriters, with no new work required.

The bill gives libraries a new right to copy and share works in the last 20 years of their term if they are no longer sold — but the same bill pushes that window 20 years further out, so libraries lose far more access than they gain.
